newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin meets PM, new battle looms over budget.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin meets PM, new battle looms over budget.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, back in the Kremlin after May Day holidays, met senior officials on Monday to discuss national security and economic reforms as his government prepared for battle over unpopular spending cuts.

In talks with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, Yeltsin focused on wage arrears -- Russia's number one social problem affecting millions of workers -- and on seeking parliamentary backing for austerity plans.
Chernomyrdin later signed government action plans for the current year and for the period to the year 2000, both in line with Yeltsin's orders to strengthen free market reforms.

Details given by Russian news agencies listed a host of projects, from introducing market mechanisms for energy monopolies and cutting the budget deficit to paying arrears in pensions by July 1 and clamping down on corruption by insisting on open tenders for federal contracts.

Deputy Prime Minister Oleg Sysuyev, one of the reformers appointed by Yeltsin in March, underlined the troubles over pensions. Itar-Tass news agency quoted him as saying efforts to clear backlogs were already behind schedule.

Yeltsin also met Ivan Rybkin, secretary of the policy-making Security Council, to discuss Moscow's delicate relations with the breakaway region of Chechnya and the development of a new doctrine of national security.
He later formally welcomed King Juan Carlos of Spain at the start of a three-day royal visit.
The flurry of engagements followed a break for the 66-year-old president, first at the Black Sea resort of Sochi and then at a country residence outside Moscow.
Yeltsin is keen to keep up the momentum from his promotion of liberals to top government jobs in March.
Chernomyrdin was expected to try to persuade the State Duma, the lower house of parliament, on May 21 to accept spending cuts aimed at bridging a wide gap between revenues and expenditure.
Mikhail Zadornov, head of the Duma's budget committee, said he had received the spending bill, which a government official said would cut about one fifth of the 1997 budget.
Zadornov told Reuters that deputies, who approved the original budget only after months of angry debate, might retaliate with calls to print money to keep its spending targets.

Russia's budget gap has been an important concern for the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which suspended disbursing a $10 billion three-year loan because of low tax revenues. Officials say they expect payments to resume this month.
Chernomyrdin said he hoped the Duma, dominated by Yeltsin's communist foes, would show "a spirit of responsibility."
The Kremlin said the Security Council would meet on May 7 to discuss a new national security doctrine, widely seen as a prerequisite for a planned overhaul of the hard-up armed forces.

Rybkin told Interfax news agency Yeltsin would meet Chechen President Aslan Maskhadov once officials completed documents charting a new relationship between Russia and the secessionist region. The two sides fought a 21-month war until last August.
Rybkin's deputy Boris Berezovsky told NTV television there had been progress in negotiations but only talks "in the near future" between the two leaders could settle the final points.
Russia has beefed up security after two bomb explosions in two southern towns near Chechnya killed four people last month.
The Chechen authorities issued an arrest warrant for radical Chechen commander Salman Raduyev, who claimed responsibility.
